name: Suma
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Moñino, Yves 1995, Le proto-gbaya: essai de linguistique comparative (Paris: Peeters), pp. 451-455 on Suma; comparative phonology of Gbaya group incl. Suma. Not online.

new_statements.quote: 1. Suma's Tone System. Suma is a 3-tone Niger-Congo language spoken in the northwestern part of the Central African Republic. Three phonological tones form lexical contrasts in words like the following: (1) kutu 'scabies of dogs & goats' / kūtū 'fog' / kútú 'certain tree Papiliona'. The three tones are also used morphologically to contrast different tenses in verbs. ... [Bradshaw 1999: 9-10] Underlyingly all verbs are toneless, and changes in aspect are marked by tone alternations. ... there is a restriction on tone in Suma such that no more than one tone per mora is allowed. ... only monosyllabic verb stems can be bimoraic.
new_statements.citation: Bradshaw, Mary M. 1995. The independent development of mid tone in Suma. Ohio State University Working Papers in Linguistics 46: 1-15 (supported by Bradshaw 1999, A crosslinguistic study of consonant-tone interaction, OSU PhD diss., sec. 2.2.1 pp. 8-10).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked in (1), PDF p. 11 = printed p. 2 of Bradshaw 1995 'The independent development of mid tone in Suma' (OSU WPL 46: 1-15): section heading is roman 'I. Suma's Tone System' (scanned '.~vstem'); text reads 'Suma is a 3-tone Niger-Congo language spoken in the northwestern part of the Central African Republic. Three phonological tones form lexical contrasts in words like the following: (1) kutu 'scabies of dogs & goats' / kutu 'fog' / kutu 'certain tree Papiliona'. The three tones are also used morphologically to contrast different tenses in verbs.' -- matches the reported quote except that the text layer drops the tone diacritics and the reader wrote '1.' for 'I.'. grep stress|accen…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Suma is described purely as a three-tone language (H, M, L; mora = tone-bearing unit, at most one tone per mora; nouns lexically toned, verbs toneless with aspect marked by tonal melodies; voiced obstruents act as depressors). None of the three accessible first-hand descriptions (Bradshaw 1995, Bradshaw 1999 sec. 2.2.1, Boyd & Sankpam 2019 introduction) says anything about word stress or accent, positive or negative.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source read.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Closest explicit statements are for neighbouring/superordinate lects, not Suma itself: Samarin 1966 p. 47 fn. 21 (Gbeya of Bossangoa: stress only a 'stylistically utilized vocal modifier', not linguistically structured; he states Suma speech 'was not studied'); Ruckstuhl 1998 sec. 5.2 'Gbaya has no phonemic stress' (gbay1287, in catalog); Moñino 1995 p. 285 (no accent/intensity/length in any of his 21 Gbaya languages, a sample that excludes Suma).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical/grammatical tone in citation forms and short phrases; tone changes under determination (nouns take final H when determined, Boyd & Sankpam 2019: IX) and in the associative construction are phrase-level tonal morphology, not accent.
new_statements.identity_note: All Suma-specific sources read (Bradshaw 1995 OSU WPL 46, Bradshaw 1999 diss. sec. 2.2.1, Boyd & Sankpam 2019) describe the Suma of the Bossangoa-Boguila area, N-W CAR (Bradshaw's fieldwork with Rick Bradshaw's Peace Corps contacts; Boyd's dictionary built on R. Bradshaw's materials) = Glottolog suma1264. The only explicit 'no accent' statements in the vicinity are for the sister lect Gbeya/Gbaya of Bossangoa (gbay1287: Samarin 1966 p. 47 fn. 21; Ruckstuhl 1998 sec. 5.2, already in the catalog) and Moñino 1995 p. 285 for his 21-language Gbaya sample, which does not include Suma (Bradshaw 1995: 1-2), although Moñino p. 16 calls the speech of the Suma of 'Bogira 'une variété de gbéyá'. Bradshaw stresses Suma differs from Gbeya in having three phonological tones (mid < *LH).

sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 1 (p. 2) describes Suma as a 3-tone language with lexical and grammatical (verb tense/aspect) tone; rest of paper is diachronic tonology vs. Moñino's 21 Gbaya languages. grep stress/accent/prominence over pp. 1-15: zero hits.

Paris/Louvain: Peeters. pp. 285, 345 (Google Books preview images on file under../gban1260/) and search-within-volume snippets for 'suma' (pp. 16, 39, 44).
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: Harvard print copy (Scan & Deliver or loan): WID Offsite Storage PL8205.M66 1995 (also: hathitrust digitized, search-only (in copyright))
sources.note: p. 285 Remarque 2: none of the 21 Gbaya languages studied 'ne présente actuellement de phénomène d'accent, d'intensité ni de longueur'. Suma is not one of the 21 (Bradshaw 1995: 1-2 says so explicitly); p. 16 snippet treats the speech of the Suma of 'Bogira as 'une variété de gbéyá'. No Suma chapter (the earlier scan note 'pp. 451-455 on Suma' is not borne out by the volume search).

sources.citation: Samarin, William J. 1966. The Gbeya language: grammar, texts, and vocabularies (UCPL 44). Berkeley: University of California Press.
sources.note: For Gbeya of Bossangoa (not Suma): p. 47 fn. 21 lists stress among 'stylistically utilized vocal modifiers' that are not linguistically structured. Introduction pp. 2-3: Suma is a mutually intelligible idiom of the district but 'Suma speech was not studied and carefully compared with the one described here'; his Suma data showed three tone levels.

sources.citation: Boyd, Raymond & Philippe Sankpam. 2019. Dictionnaire suma-français(-anglais). Orléans: Laboratoire Ligérien de Linguistique; web publication ('premier jet'), introduction 16 pp. + 12 letter files (Glottolog ref 601361, 952 pp.).
sources.note: Nothing. 'Informations pratiques' pp. VII-IX (rendered and read visually; text layer defective): alphabet with three tone marks on short/long, oral/nasal vowels; vowel-sequence and semivowel conventions; nominal tone schemes change under determination to end in H; perfective = -a plus mid scheme. No accent/stress remark.

sources.citation: Bradshaw, Mary M. 1999. A crosslinguistic study of consonant-tone interaction. PhD dissertation, The Ohio State University (OhioLINK ETD osu1392896719).
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.2.1 'Suma' (pp. 8-10, read as page images): voiced obstruents are depressors inserting L; verbs underlyingly toneless with aspect marked by tone; 'no more than one tone per mora'; only monosyllabic verb stems bimoraic. Vita pp. vii-viii lists all her Suma publications.
